impecunious

im-puh-KYOO-nee-us · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Impecunious is having little or no money.

As an impecunious graduate student, he lived on instant noodles and never once turned on the heat in winter.

Example

The impecunious knight in the old story had a noble title but not a single coin left to his name.

Impecunious describes the plain fact of having no money -- it says nothing about how the person got that way.

Your Turn

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

penniless: Penniless means having no money at all -- absolute zero, often after losing everything at once. Impecunious is a shade softer and slower: an impecunious person lives with little or no money as an ongoing condition, scraping by rather than stripped bare in a single blow.

broke: Broke is the informal, everyday word for being out of money right now, and it usually suggests a short stretch -- broke until payday. Impecunious describes the long haul: little or no money not for a week but as a lasting state of life.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

affluent: having a great deal of wealth

wealthy: having a great deal of money

Where it sits · how deep the lack of money runs — short on cash → impecunious → destitute

short on cash vs. impecunious: Being short on cash is far milder than being impecunious: short on cash means one tight week, while an impecunious person has almost no money and cannot cover basic needs.

destitute vs. impecunious: Destitute goes a step beyond impecunious: an impecunious person scrapes by with almost nothing, while a destitute one has lost even the basics -- no home, no food, no fallback at all.

Word Choice

Impecunious names the state of being poor. Improvidence names the careless habit that can cause that state -- the two are cause and effect, not synonyms.
